h1: Customer service and complaints roles at beer companies
title: Customer Service Roles at Beer Companies | Craft Beer School
desc: What customer service and complaints staff do at beer companies, how complaints are investigated and the skills that help.
teaser: A complaint about flat beer or a strange smell is a quality report in disguise. Someone has to read it properly.
standfirst: Customer service teams at beer companies handle orders, queries and complaints from bars, retailers and drinkers. The best of them understand enough brewing to tell a real fault from a storage problem. Here is what the role involves.
sections:
Every brewery gets complaints. A can that gushes, a bottle that tastes of cardboard, a keg that pours flat, a label that peels off in the ice bucket. Each one costs the brewery something, but each also tells it something. A good customer service team turns complaints into information the brewers and quality team can act on.

In a large beer company, this is a dedicated team with procedures and targets. In a craft brewery it is often the sales coordinator, the taproom manager or the founder answering emails at night. The work is the same either way: listen, record, investigate and respond.
What the job involves day to day

Customer service at a beer company covers more than complaints:

  • Taking and tracking orders from distributors, bars and retailers.
  • Answering questions about availability, pricing, delivery and products.
  • Logging complaints with enough detail for someone to investigate.
  • Arranging replacements or credit within company policy.
  • Reporting patterns to quality, sales and logistics teams.

The last task is the one that adds most value. One complaint about flat beer is a complaint. Five from the same batch code is a quality problem.
The batch code is the most important detail

Every can, bottle and keg should carry a batch code or a best before date that links it to a production run. When a complaint comes in, the first job is to get that code. With it, the quality team can pull retained samples from the same batch, check the lab records and see whether other complaints share it.

Without it, investigation is guesswork. Train yourself to ask for the code, a photo of the product and where and how it was stored. Those three facts solve more complaints than any amount of apology.
Telling a brewing fault from a handling fault

Many complaints are not brewing faults at all. Beer left in the sun goes stale or picks up a skunky note from light. Kegs stored warm or connected at the wrong gas pressure pour as foam. Glasses washed with greasy cloths kill the head. A customer service person who knows the difference can save the brewery from chasing problems that started at the outlet.

Common complaints and their usual suspects:

  • Gushing. Over-carbonation, contamination by wild yeast or a warm, shaken pack.
  • Flat beer. Low carbonation, a leaking seal or wrong dispense pressure.
  • Cardboard or papery taste. Oxidation, often from age or warm storage.
  • Buttery taste. Diacetyl, from fermentation or bacteria.
  • Skunky aroma. Light damage, especially in clear or green glass.

Our guide to beer off-flavours goes through the common faults and where they come from.

Most people who complain want to be heard and want the problem fixed. Reply quickly, thank them, ask the right questions and tell them what happens next. Do not admit a fault before it is investigated. Do not argue that the beer is fine before anyone has tasted it.

Follow company policy on replacements or credit. Keep records of every case. Some complaints, such as a foreign object in a bottle or a suspected safety issue, need to go straight to the quality team and may need to be handled under food safety rules. Know your escalation route before you need it.

Tone matters in writing as much as on the phone. A short reply that says "we have passed your photos and the code to our quality team and will come back to you within two working days" does more than a long apology. Then keep the promise. A complaint answered well often turns an annoyed drinker into a loyal one.
Why brewing knowledge helps the job

Customer service staff who understand beer stand out. They write better complaint reports, they spot patterns sooner and they can explain to a bar manager why a keg is foaming without sounding scripted. They also move more easily into quality, sales or technical roles, because they have already learned the product from its failures. Our guide to data and analytics jobs in breweries shows another route, since complaint logs are one of the richest data sets a brewery holds.

The gap for most people in these roles is not empathy or organisation. It is the technical vocabulary to describe what went wrong and why.

Over time, a well kept complaint log shows things no single case reveals. One outlet that always reports flat beer probably has a dispense problem. One month with more cardboard complaints may point at a hot spell in the supply chain. Reading the log this way is how customer service starts to shape what the brewery does.

Your first step: take the last ten complaints your team logged, sort them by type and batch code in a spreadsheet and see whether any batch or outlet appears more than once.
faqs: What details should be collected in a beer complaint?
At minimum the batch code or best before date, a photo of the product, where it was bought and how it was stored. With the batch code, the quality team can pull retained samples and check records.
Are all beer complaints caused by brewing faults?
No. Many come from storage, transport or dispense: heat, light, wrong gas pressure or dirty glasses. Knowing the difference saves time and points the investigation in the right direction.
Can customer service lead to a quality role?
Yes. People who learn the technical side of complaints often move into quality, technical sales or product roles, because they already understand how the product fails.
